sentences.text: The tidal range at Kerlouan is eight metres on a big spring and that number is the reason for everything about the place.
Eight metres means the harbour is a harbour for about five hours out of every twelve and a field of mud for the rest.
It means the wall is enormous.

It means every boat there has legs, and the whole of the working life of that village is arranged around a table of numbers that has been published in an almanac since 1839 and that is now on everybody's phone.
Maëlle grew up inside that arrangement the way other children grow up inside a school timetable.
Meals moved.

Her father's working day started at a different hour every day of her childhood and moved fifty minutes later each time, and she could tell you the state of the tide from the smell coming off the harbour before she could tell the time.
Everybody in Kerlouan does that arithmetic constantly and nobody there thinks of it as arithmetic.
The tables are extremely good.
Maëlle would like that said first, because the story sounds otherwise like it is against them.
They are astronomy.

The tide is the moon and the sun pulling on a rotating planet, and that is a solved problem, and the tables for Kerlouan are accurate to about four minutes and eleven centimetres a century in advance.
What the tables do not have is the weather.
A hard low pressure system lifts the whole sea.
Wind piles it up against a coast or holds it off.

On a bad day in Brittany the actual water can be sixty or seventy centimetres above what the table says, and once in a generation a great deal more than that, and the table cannot know because the table was calculated in 1974.
Which is what the shoal is for.
There is a bar across the mouth of that harbour and on the flood there is a shoal of mullet over it, and there has been for as long as the village has records of anything.
Two or three hundred fish, grey, unremarkable, doing the entirely normal thing that mullet do in an estuary.
They are grey mullet and they are the least regarded fish on that coast.
Nobody eats them if there is anything else.

They come in on the flood to work the mud and they go out on the ebb and they have done that in every estuary in Europe since before there were estuaries in Europe, and there is nothing whatever unusual about the shoal at Kerlouan except that people used to look at it.
And where they sit tells you the water.
